fa: Fred Beckey, Dallas Kloke and Reed Tindall, July 19, 1978
overview: A glacier route ascending the peak's northeast side, near the Nohokomeen Glacier basin.
beta: One of Jack Mountain's established routes; no grade has been recorded for this line.

first_pass.evidence: Northeast Glacier (Beckey party, 1978) is listed without a grade; the AAJ describes a badly broken north-side glacier where objective danger forced the party onto a ridge to the right.
first_pass.note: No published difficulty; Class 3 is a reading of a broken glacier plus Jack's class 3-4 summit ridges.

overview: A Class 3 scramble along Klawatti's north ridge from the Klawatti-Austera Col, working around a rock tower nicknamed 'The Smokestack' before finishing on the summit crest.
beta: From the 7,900-ft Klawatti-Austera Col (an easy side-trip from Klawatti Col), gain the lower part of the north ridge — easiest on its east side — and scramble Class 3 terrain to a rock tower nicknamed 'The Smokestack' (roughly 8,400 ft). Circumnavigate the Smokestack on its west side via a short gully to regain the ridge crest, then follow the crest to the summit. About 1 hour from the Klawatti-Austera Col, up to 2 hours from the main Klawatti Col.

first_pass.evidence: From the Klawatti-Austera col, Class 3 scrambling leads to The Smokestack, which is bypassed; the record says Class 4 in spots.
first_pass.note: Top of the record's own 'Class 3 (Class 4 in spots)'; no source gives a single crux grade.

rock_grade: Class 4 (slabby rock once the snow melts)
fa: Lloyd Anderson, Karl Boyer, Tom Gorton - July 7, 1940 (also the peak's first ascent)
overview: Klawatti Peak is a nunatak — an ice-surrounded rock summit — ringed by the Klawatti Glacier (east), McAllister Glacier (northwest), and Inspiration Glacier (south) in the North Cascades National Park high country. First climbed in 1940 by Lloyd Anderson, Karl Boyer, and Tom Gorton, it lies between Eldorado Peak and Austera Peak/Dorado Needle and is reached only after a full day or more of committing glacier travel. The Southeast Face route climbs directly off the Klawatti Glacier, crossing a ber
beta: Grade III alpine route requiring mixed climbing technique. Approach via Klawatti Glacier from the west with one short Class 4-5 rock step over the bergschrund followed by several hundred feet of 40-55 degree snow. Crampons, ice axe, pickets, 60m rope, and single rack to 2 inch are essential. Allow 1-2 hours for climbing depending on amount of roped climbing.

first_pass.evidence: South/SE face from Klawatti Col: 45-50° snow through a constriction (icy at times, bergschrund bridges) in early season; later it melts out to slabs with a moat.
first_pass.note: No source confirms the 5.2 / low-5th in the record's breakdown. In snow condition it is steep snow (Class 3 by the brief); Class 4 is kept for the late-season slabby rock.

face: East spur of Lemah Two — the upper and taller of the spur's two rock towers
fa: Donald Goodman and John Mason, August 8, 1982 (upper tower of the two on Lemah Two's east spur)
overview: A separate rock tower (~7,000 ft) on the eastern spur of Lemah Two — the upper of two towers there, the lower being more massive.
beta: Goatshead Spire is documented only by its location (Lemah Two's east spur), approximate elevation, and first-ascent party/date; no grade, pitch count, or detailed route description has been published.

first_pass.evidence: Goatshead Spire (Goodman/Mason, 1982) is listed with no grade; MP notes that Lemah's summits all have class 4-low 5th routes.
first_pass.note: No published grade anywhere; 5.0 is the low-5th default for a rock tower on this massif.

route: West Face - West Rib (Lichtenhorn / West Peak)
rock_grade: Class 3 with short class 4 steps on the rib; the summit spire is either a loose class 3 wrap-around or a solid low-5th-class direct finish
face: West Face / West Rib of The Lichtenhorn (west peak)
overview: A little-documented technical rock line up the west face and rib of Lichtenberg's western sub-summit (the ~5,800+ ft 'Lichtenhorn'), the rocky pinnacle overlooking Lake Valhalla, approached via Lichtenberg Pass and descended via the northeast slope.
beta: Historic climbing-club parties describe an off-trail approach from the Old Lake Valhalla/Lake Janus trailhead via Union Gap and Lichtenberg Pass, then a rock climb up the west face and west rib of the west peak, with descent down the easier northeast slope back toward the start. Little is known about grade and protection; treat this as an obscure, lightly-traveled line rather than a well-established route.
breakdown: Section 1 - PCT saddle to the base of the west rib: Class 2
Section 2 - the west rib: Class 3, short class 4 steps
Section 3 - summit spire of The Lichtenhorn: Class 3 (wrap-around) or low 5th class (direct)

first_pass.evidence: Only a trip-report entry (rock climb via West Face-West Rib) found, with no rating; the spire's wrap-around is reported elsewhere as loose Class 3.
first_pass.note: Taken from the record's own rock_grade: Class 3 with short Class 4 steps, then the Class 3 wrap-around. The low-5th direct finish is an option, not the normal line. The record has no headline grade.

fa: Fred Beckey, Wesley Grande, Herb Staley, John Rupley — July 22, 1956
overview: Lincoln Peak's SW Face route, known as the 'X Couloir' (sometimes referenced as 'X Couloir – Emancipation Proclamation'), is the historic line up this seldom-climbed, seriously loose Black Buttes summit. First climbed by Fred Beckey, Wesley Grande, John Rupley, and Herb Staley on July 22, 1956, it was the only documented route to the summit until a 2015 first ascent opened a second line on the NW Face. Only about a dozen ascents are known; the peak is guarded by near-vertical walls on every side
beta: The historic standard route on Lincoln Peak; the only other line is a rarely formed northwest-face ice route. Approach via Rankin Creek Basin from FS Road 38. Technical snow and ice climbing with significant avalanche risk. Route comprises multiple sections: 30-40 degree initial snowfields, crux serac obstacle requiring 70-85 degree ice climbing (50 feet high), hidden gully with 2-4 foot deep runnels, narrow exposed snow aretes with steep drop-offs, and final 50-degree gully to summit rocks. Cli

first_pass.evidence: Trip reports: X Couloir is 60+ degree exposed snow/ice with a narrow crux gully near 75 degrees, climbed with tools and screws; no published ice grade.
first_pass.note: No source gives an ice grade; AI3 is a mapping from the ~75-degree gully (the record says AI3+). The headline 'III-IV' is a commitment numeral, not a grade. A commitment of VI is impossible for this one-day route (about 9 hours in TRs).

overview: Little Mac Spire is a minor rock pinnacle in the Southern Pickets, immediately adjacent to East McMillan Spire within the McMillan Spires group, North Cascades National Park. It is rarely climbed as a stand-alone objective — most ascents happen when parties already engaged with the McMillan Spires or a full Southern Pickets enchainment tag the summit en route, then continue across to a horn and rappel into the gully below East McMillan Spire. It is reached via the Terror Basin approach from the
beta: The southwest-facing route provides technical alpine climbing with high-quality rock. Approximately 800 feet of climbing to summit with exposed sections requiring careful route-finding.

first_pass.evidence: Little Mac's south side is described only as low 5th-class; no numbered route grade was found.
first_pass.note: Kept the record's 5.4. Low 5th is the only rating sources give.

face: South side of Little Sister, above the 6,240+ ft col that separates it from Cinderella Peak
fa: Unknown (first known ski descent: Mark Allen, May 2007)
overview: A snow and rock gully on Little Sister's south side, reached by climbing to the col southeast of the summit and traversing onto the south aspect. It has been skied during a traverse of the whole Twin Sisters Range and climbed in winter as a moderate snow gully with a bit of mixed ground near the summit.
beta: This line was skied as part of a multi-day (May 12-14) south-to-north ski traverse of the Twin Sisters Range by Chris Simmons, Mark Allen, Greg Balco, and Paul Kimbrough. On the second day one of them skied Little Sister's South Couloir, singled out as the trip's best line. The traverse's technical crux - about 40 m of 4th-class rock, 100+ m of 50-degree ice, then 100+ m of rappelling ending in a fixed rappel with a knot pass - came later, on a crossing of the range near South Twin Sister, not o
breakdown: Snow to the col: Steep snow
South-side gully: 3rd class snow and rock

first_pass.evidence: Only a ski descent of Little Sister's South Face Couloir on a Twin Sisters haute route was found; no rating.
first_pass.note: Taken from the record's own breakdown: steep snow plus 3rd-class snow and rock, mapped to Class 3. The record has no headline grade.

face: West Face of Little Sister — the broad wall on the far side of the peak from the Green Creek Glacier, reached over the Sister Divide as part of the Green Creek Circuit
overview: The largest wall of generally sound rock in the Twin Sisters group: a long, low-commitment line of consistent 4th and low-5th-class climbing that can be soloed, simul-climbed, or pitched out over up to seven pitches.
beta: Climb the West Face on consistent 4th and low-5th-class rock; expect loose debris on the lower ledges but improving rock quality and exposure higher up. Route-finding variations are common and affect the difficulty encountered.

first_pass.evidence: MP: West Face 'Easy 5th', with no number anywhere.
first_pass.note: Low 5th with no number, so 5.0 per the rule.

face: South (county-line) ridge from the Sentinel Peak col
overview: A remote, seldom-visited summit on the divide between the Cascade Pass and Dome Peak country, Lizard Mountain rises above the White Rock Lakes basin along the classic Ptarmigan Traverse -- one of the North Cascades' premier glaciated high routes. Most parties encounter it as a half-day side-scramble from a White Rock Lakes camp (reached via Lizard Pass), roughly three to four days into a north-to-south traverse from Cascade Pass; there is no dedicated trailhead or day-hike approach. The Class 3
beta: Lizard Mountain has no trailhead of its own — parties reach it only by first completing several days of the Ptarmigan Traverse's off-trail, glaciated high route, then scrambling from a camp near Lizard Col. The summit push itself is straightforward (class 3) once you're on site; the real crux of the route is the multi-day glacier approach to get there.

first_pass.evidence: Only peak listings and logged ascents found; no published route rating.
first_pass.note: Kept the record's own Class 3 (direct; Class 2 by the talus-bench bypass).

face: Upper Richardson Glacier to the East Ridge
fa: Rodney Glisan, H.H. Prouty, Winthrop Stone, C.W. Whittlesey (Mazamas) — August 13, 1911
overview: Luahna Peak (8,445-8,450 ft) is the second-highest summit of the Dakobed (Chiwawa) Range, immediately northwest of Clark Mountain, deep in the Boulder Creek/Napeequa River country of the Glacier Peak Wilderness. It is a rarely visited top-100 Washington peak, first climbed August 13, 1911 by a Mazamas party (Rodney Glisan, H.H. Prouty, Winthrop Stone, C.W. Whittlesey). Because the approach alone consumes most of a day, most modern parties climb Luahna together with Clark Mountain via the connect
beta: The standard line crosses the upper Richardson Glacier from the col west of Clark Mountain to reach Luahna's East Ridge, then follows the ridge crest west to the summit. Most of the ridge is easy scrambling, but a short, steep step low on it goes at about low Class 4 and is often avoided on ledges and a parallel gully to one side. The glacier has been thinning and breaking up, snow and loose rock persist well into summer, and the route is commonly combined with adjacent Clark Mountain in a singl

first_pass.evidence: Luahna's summit scramble is reported as Class 2-3 (Pilz/Walrus side); one TR found a direct south-side line about 4th class.
first_pass.note: Top of the record's Class 2-3. No source names an 'East Slopes' route as such.

overview: A short, easy final pitch of broken rock and slab to Lundin's summit from the saddle between Lundin and East Lundin, reached via a considerably longer approach over Red Pass.
beta: Broken rock, past a slab section and up another small section of featured rock to the summit. Three large installed bolts aid navigation, and multiple easy variations are available.

first_pass.evidence: MP: East Ridge 'Easy 5th'; no numbered grade found.
first_pass.note: Low 5th with no number, so 5.0 per the rule.

rock_grade: Easy 5th (Class 4 with a short low-5th crux)
overview: Lundin Peak is a jagged, three-horned summit — the westernmost horn is the true summit — on the ridge connecting Snoqualmie Mountain (6,278 ft) to Red Mountain, immediately north of Snoqualmie Pass in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. Formerly named 'Snoqualmie Little Sister,' it was renamed in 1931 to honor district forest ranger John Lundin. Short approaches from I-90 and a mix of scrambling/low-5th rock make it one of the most popular half-day alpine objectives near Seattle, but the summit block i
beta: The West Ridge is a compact, sub-1,000-foot ridge climb rated Easy 5th/Grade II. Climbers gain the ridge crest from a notch, then move over generally sound blocky rock, mostly Class 3-4 scrambling with a crux slabby depression rated Class 4/5.0 guarding the final approach to the summit. It's frequently used as a first alpine rock climb, though route-finding, some cliffing, and loose talus mean it should not be treated as a casual scramble.

first_pass.evidence: MP: Easy 5th, Grade II; mostly Class 3 with a 'Class 4/5' slabby-depression crux.
first_pass.note: Low 5th with no number, so 5.0 per the rule; the record's 'Class 4-5.0' tops out at the same value.

overview: The original 1941 line up Lundin's south face, rising from the headwaters of Commonwealth Creek. Several low-5th-class pitches lead to a slab; the final pitch above it is steeper before topping out near the true (westernmost) summit.
beta: Climb the South Face of Lundin, which rises from the headwaters of Commonwealth Creek. Several low-5th pitches lead to a slab; the final pitch after this is steeper.

first_pass.evidence: MP: South Face (Crooks/Kennedy 1941) Easy 5th, Grade II, 4 pitches; several low-5th pitches, a steeper final pitch, no numbers.
first_pass.note: Low 5th with no number, so 5.0 per the rule. The record's breakdown (5.4-5.6) is more specific than any source found.
